mcqs.question: In the BFS implementation, why is a neighbor marked visited at the moment it's enqueued, rather than when it's later dequeued?
options: Marking on dequeue would make the algorithm run in O(V^2) instead of O(V+E)
It has no effect on correctness either way, only on code style
Marking on enqueue prevents the same node from being added to the queue multiple times before it's ever processed
Enqueue-time marking is required so the queue can be implemented as a stack instead
mcqs.explanation: If marking happens only on dequeue, a node reachable via multiple edges can be enqueued several times before any of those copies is processed, wasting work and, in some variants, corrupting the result. It's a correctness issue, not a complexity-class change, and has nothing to do with swapping the queue for a stack.

mcqs.question: Why does BFS guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph while DFS does not?
options: DFS is slower than BFS in the worst case, so it explores fewer nodes
BFS processes all nodes at distance k before any node at distance k+1, so the first time a node is reached is guaranteed to be via the fewest possible edges
DFS only works correctly on trees, not general graphs
BFS uses less memory than DFS, which is what guarantees the shortest path
mcqs.explanation: BFS's queue enforces strict level-by-level processing, so a node can never be first reached via a longer path while a shorter path to it remains unexplored. DFS has no such ordering guarantee — its exploration order depends on neighbor iteration order, not distance, so it can stumble onto a long path before a shorter one. Both traversals have identical time complexity and both work on general graphs; memory usage doesn't determine path length guarantees.

mcqs.question: You need to find, for every cell in a grid, its distance to the nearest of several "source" cells. What's the most efficient BFS-based approach?
options: Seed the BFS queue with all source cells at distance 0 simultaneously, then run one combined BFS
Run a separate single-source BFS from each source cell and take the minimum result at each cell
Run DFS from each source cell instead, since BFS only supports one starting point
Sort the source cells first, then BFS from only the first one
mcqs.explanation: Multi-source BFS seeds all sources into the queue at once, flooding outward simultaneously, and the level-by-level guarantee still holds — now measured as distance to the nearest source — in a single O(V+E) pass. Running a separate BFS per source and taking the minimum works but repeats far more work than necessary; BFS supports multiple starting points natively, and sorting sources doesn't apply here.

mcqs.question: You're searching a very wide but shallow graph (many nodes per level, few levels total). Which traversal is likely to use less peak memory?
options: DFS, since its stack depth is bounded by the graph's depth, which is small here, while BFS's queue can hold an entire wide level at once
BFS, since it always uses less memory than DFS regardless of graph shape
Both use identical memory in every case
Neither — memory usage depends only on the total number of edges
mcqs.explanation: DFS's memory footprint scales with depth (one stack frame per node on the current path), while BFS's scales with the widest level it needs to hold in the queue at once — on a wide, shallow graph, that makes DFS's peak memory much smaller. Neither traversal's memory use is a fixed constant independent of the graph's shape, and total edge count alone doesn't determine peak memory for either.

mcqs.question: A candidate uses DFS to solve a problem asking for the minimum number of moves between two states in an unweighted graph. The code runs and returns an answer on every test case tried. What's the risk?
options: DFS is fine here, since it visits the same set of reachable nodes as BFS would
DFS may find a longer path first purely due to neighbor iteration order, silently returning a non-minimal answer on some graph shapes even though it never crashes
The code will throw a runtime error on graphs with cycles
DFS runs in a higher time complexity than BFS, so it will simply time out on large graphs
mcqs.explanation: DFS has no ordering guarantee tying discovery order to path length, so it can find and return a longer path before ever considering a shorter one — a bug that produces a plausible-looking but wrong answer, with no crash and no obvious signal, only surfacing on inputs shaped to expose it. Both traversals share the same O(V+E) complexity and both handle cycles correctly with a visited set; the issue is purely about which path is found first, not runtime behavior.

mcqs.question: A BFS implementation marks a node visited only when it's dequeued, not when it's enqueued. On a graph where a node has multiple incoming edges from already-enqueued nodes, what happens?
options: The traversal crashes with a KeyError or similar
Nothing changes — visited marking timing has no effect on the result
The queue silently converts into a stack, changing the traversal into DFS
The same node can be enqueued multiple times before it's ever processed, wasting work and potentially corrupting results that depend on discovery counts
mcqs.explanation: Without enqueue-time marking, every path that reaches an unprocessed node before it's dequeued will enqueue it again, since nothing yet flags it as already queued — this wastes work and can break any logic that assumes each node is discovered exactly once. It doesn't crash, doesn't change the underlying data structure, and definitely isn't a no-op — this is a classic, subtle BFS correctness bug.
